lessons.title: FGCP session pickup: what survives a failover, what does not, and why heartbeat capacity matters
lessons.summary: Session pickup extends FGCP failover beyond interface and configuration ownership. It replicates session state so the newly elected primary can continue eligible transit flows rather than forcing every client to create a new connection.
lessons.body:
Purpose and boundary. FGCP can elect a new primary when the current primary fails, but election alone does not preserve application conversations. Session pickup is the separate state-replication function that keeps the secondary's session table current. It is not a promise that every connection survives. The 8.0 Administration Guide says session pickup is not enabled by default; when enabled, the primary synchronizes its TCP session table to the other cluster members as new sessions are created. After failover, the new primary uses those entries to continue processing eligible sessions from their last known state.

What is replicated. Think of the session table as the data-plane memory needed to recognize an existing flow: its endpoints and protocol, timers, policy association, and the state required for forwarding and translation. The primary sends session updates over the HA synchronization path, normally carried by heartbeat interfaces unless a supported session-sync interface is configured. This is distinct from configuration synchronization: a perfectly synchronized configuration does not prove that the secondary has the live session state required for continuity.

Protocol scope matters. The standard FortiGate guide documents TCP session pickup. UDP and ICMP do not have the same connection-oriented state by default; enable connectionless pickup when those flows need continuity. A minimal configuration is:

config system ha
    set session-pickup enable
    set session-pickup-connectionless enable
end

Do not enable connectionless synchronization merely because it exists. It increases state-update work and should be justified by the applications that need it. Specialized platforms and FGSP deployments expose additional options, including expectation-session synchronization; those options are not interchangeable with the baseline FGCP setting. Keep the platform and HA mode attached to every command example.

Inspection and termination caveats. Session pickup does not make cluster-terminated services transparent. Management sessions such as HTTPS GUI, SSH, SNMP and logging, and VPN or explicit-proxy sessions terminated on the FortiGate generally have to reconnect. Proxy-based security-profile sessions are not supported for session failover. Flow-based sessions can be resumed, but the documented limitation is important: after failover, a resumed flow-based session is not inspected again. An engineer must therefore distinguish “the TCP socket continued” from “the original inspection pipeline continued.”

Capacity and convergence. Session synchronization consumes heartbeat bandwidth. The amount depends on connection rate because new sessions and session updates must be copied. A failover or a member rejoining the cluster can create a burst while session state is synchronized. A low-throughput heartbeat link can lengthen convergence even when heartbeats themselves look healthy. Where supported, a dedicated session-sync interface can move this traffic away from the heartbeat path; validate that interface design and the model's supported topology before changing it.

Verification. Confirm the HA mode and primary/secondary roles first, then inspect session-pickup configuration on the cluster. Use diagnose sys ha status to establish which unit is primary and whether members are healthy. Use diagnose sys session list with a source/destination filter to confirm that the test flow exists before failover and is present on the new primary afterward. Observe heartbeat-interface utilization during a controlled failover. A successful HA election proves control-plane failover; it does not prove that a particular session class was synchronized.

Operational example. A long-running TCP transfer resets after a planned failover while ordinary web browsing recovers. First identify whether the transfer crossed a proxy-based inspection profile or a flow-based profile, then confirm session pickup and heartbeat capacity. If only the GUI and IPsec VPN sessions reset, that can be expected because those services terminate on the cluster. Do not “fix” this by increasing heartbeat bandwidth until you have proved the affected flow is eligible for session pickup.

Engineer’s takeaway: validate continuity by protocol and inspection mode, not by a single successful ping or HA status indicator.
lessons.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FGCP primary-to-secondary session-table replication; TCP session pickup; optional connectionless UDP/ICMP synchronization; multicast route TTL synchronization; proxy-flow inspection limitation
lessons.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: new session enters primary session table -> session state is copied over HA heartbeat/session-sync path -> failover elects new primary -> synchronized entry continues from last known state; cluster-terminated sessions restart independently
lessons.evidence_pattern: config system ha session-pickup; diagnose sys ha status; diagnose sys session list; heartbeat interface throughput and session table parity; compare proxy versus flow-based policy path
lessons.remediation_path: enable session-pickup only after capacity review; separately decide connectionless synchronization; move sync traffic to dedicated session-sync interfaces when supported; keep proxy-inspected expectations out of continuity claims; validate failover by protocol and policy mode
lessons.question_fingerprint: distinguish synchronized transit sessions from cluster-terminated VPN/management sessions and identify why a flow-based session can resume without continuing inspection
lessons.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: two-node FGCP primary/secondary with HA1/HA2 sync arrow, client/server transit path, separate cluster-terminated VPN endpoint path, failover promotion

lessons.title: IPS provisioning templates: global versus VDOM-scoped objects and target-aware assignment
lessons.summary: An IPS template is a provisioning object that groups global IPS settings with VDOM-scoped IPS configuration. The target VDOM changes what FortiManager copies, so assignment success is not proof that every object reached the intended scope.
lessons.body:
Purpose. FortiManager IPS templates let an IPS administrator define a repeatable set of intrusion-prevention settings and assign it to a managed FortiGate or device group within an ADOM. The important design point is that the template is not a flat blob. FortiManager exposes three object scopes: IPS Global for global settings, and System IPS plus IPS Settings for VDOM-based configuration. That distinction determines which parts are meaningful on a particular target.

Object model and transaction. The administrator creates the template under Device Manager > Provisioning Templates > IPS Templates, enters a name and description, and configures one or more of the three IPS objects. The template can be edited, cloned, or deleted. Assignment is a separate action: select the template, choose Assign to Device/Group, and move the intended devices into the selected target list. FortiManager then applies the applicable objects to the device/VDOM configuration database as part of the provisioning/install workflow. The template's existence and assignment record are therefore two different facts; neither alone proves that the final device configuration contains every intended object.

The root/mgmt exception. Fortinet documents a specific target rule: when copying an IPS template to a device VDOM whose target is root or mgmt, only IPS Global is copied. The VDOM-scoped System IPS and IPS Settings objects are not copied by that operation. This is an easy way to create a misleading result: the template appears assigned, the global IPS setting is present, but a VDOM-specific expectation is absent. The right response is not to keep reinstalling blindly; first verify which VDOM was selected and which object scope the target supports.

Administrative scope. A full administrator reaches the template through Device Manager > Provisioning Templates. A restricted IPS administrator can work from Intrusion Prevention > IPS Templates, subject to the administrator profile. If the menu is missing, check the administrator's feature access before assuming that the ADOM or feature is unavailable. This separation also supports delegated IPS operations without granting broad policy-package administration.

Configuration workflow. Build the template with a deliberate scope matrix. Put settings intended for the whole FortiGate in IPS Global. Put per-VDOM behavior in System IPS and IPS Settings. Assign it to a device group only when the group has a consistent VDOM design; otherwise use explicit device targets and record the VDOM mapping. Before installation, review the policy/device install preview and the generated diff. The target VDOM, not the template label, is the authority for deciding which object sections should appear.

Verification. In FortiManager, inspect the template contents and assignment table. In the install wizard, review the device/VDOM target and the configuration diff. After installation, inspect the managed device database and the FortiGate's IPS configuration in the relevant VDOM. If only IPS Global appears on root or mgmt, that can be the documented behavior rather than a failed install. If a non-root VDOM is missing its objects, compare the selected target, ADOM version, feature visibility, and install diff before changing the template.

Operational example. A security team creates one IPS template for a multi-VDOM FortiGate and assigns it to a group. The root VDOM shows the global IPS configuration, while an application VDOM lacks its per-VDOM IPS settings. The engineer checks the assignment target and discovers the template was applied to root only. The correction is to target the intended VDOM and verify the device database diff, not to duplicate global settings in a second template.

Engineer’s takeaway: treat IPS Global, System IPS, and IPS Settings as separate scopes, and verify the VDOM target before interpreting a successful assignment.
lessons.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: IPS template packages IPS Global global settings plus VDOM-scoped System IPS and IPS Settings; assignment to device or device group; root/mgmt target copies only IPS Global
lessons.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: create template in ADOM -> configure selected IPS object scopes -> assign template to device/device group -> FortiManager maps applicable global and VDOM objects to device database -> install/verify target-specific configuration
lessons.evidence_pattern: template assignment list; device/VDOM target; install preview/diff; resulting IPS Global, System IPS, and IPS Settings values on target
lessons.remediation_path: separate global and VDOM intent; assign to explicit device groups/VDOMs; verify target VDOM; inspect install preview and device-side configuration; do not infer VDOM object deployment from template assignment alone
lessons.question_fingerprint: identify why a root or mgmt VDOM receives only IPS Global and choose the correct target-aware verification
lessons.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiManager ADOM template branching into global IPS object and two VDOM object sets, with root/mgmt branch receiving global-only

lessons.title: Asset Identity Center: building endpoint and end-user identity from Fabric data sources
lessons.summary: Asset Identity Center is a normalized identity view built from selected Fabric telemetry. Its data-source rules are per ADOM and have precedence, so a missing endpoint can be a source-selection problem rather than a logging problem.
lessons.body:
Purpose. FortiAnalyzer Asset Identity Center consolidates endpoint and end-user identity clues from Fabric logs and connectors into an Asset Identity List and Identity List. It is not simply a log search page. The feature decides which sources are allowed to contribute identity observations, then presents the resulting asset/user view for dashboards and correlation. Data-source configuration is performed per ADOM, so an identity visible in one ADOM is not proof that the source is enabled in another.

Supported sources and defaults. The 8.0 Administration Guide documents FortiGate Log, FortiClient Log, FortiMail Log, FortiWeb Log, FortiNAC Log, and EMS Connector sources. FortiGate, FortiClient, FortiWeb, and FortiNAC identification is enabled by default for their documented device scope; FortiMail log identification and EMS Connector identification are disabled by default and must be explicitly included/enabled. The source type controls which filters are available: device selection for log sources, excluded subnets for FortiGate/FortiWeb/FortiNAC, included domains for FortiMail, and connector selection for EMS.

Rule precedence is operationally significant. A rule for an individual device has priority over a rule for “all devices.” Suppose all FortiGate logs are enabled, but a device-specific entry for one firewall is switched OFF. That firewall's identity data remains excluded even though the broad all-device rule is ON. When duplicate data-source entries are attempted for the same device or connector, FortiAnalyzer warns that a source already exists and offers an override. These are deliberate precedence and conflict controls; they should be inspected before changing log forwarding.

Configure the source. Enter a Fabric ADOM, open Fabric View > Asset Identity Center > Asset Identity List, and select Data Sources. Create the source, choose its type, set Status ON, and select the relevant devices, subnets, domains, or EMS connector. Use the narrowest useful inclusion/exclusion rule. Broadly excluding a subnet can suppress identity for many legitimate endpoints; disabling a source at the ADOM level removes all contribution from that source in that ADOM.

EMS vulnerability enrichment has additional dependencies. Create the EMS connector in the Fabric ADOM. FortiAnalyzer automatically creates the Update Asset, Identity and Vulnerability in Sequence playbook after the first connector is configured. Enable the playbook; it calls the EMS API, inserts Fabric/SIEM logs, and is scheduled daily by default. Add that connector as an EMS Connector data source in Asset Identity Center, then add EMS as an authorized device in Device Manager. The connector existing in the automation page is not enough if the source is disabled or the EMS device is not authorized.

Evidence and limits. Inspect the Data Sources dialog for source type, status, device scope, excluded subnets, included domains, and selected connectors. Compare the Asset/Identity List with the source logs for the same ADOM and time window. For EMS, check connector status, playbook execution, authorized-device status, and the automatically assigned EMS log parser. A populated vulnerability dashboard proves the enrichment pipeline produced data; an empty dashboard does not by itself prove that the EMS endpoint has no vulnerabilities.

Troubleshooting example. An endpoint appears in FortiGate traffic logs but not in Asset Identity List. Check the ADOM first, then source enablement, device-specific rules, and excluded subnets. If the endpoint is managed by EMS, verify the connector, playbook run, authorized-device status, and EMS data-source selection. Change one filter at a time and confirm the resulting identity record rather than enabling every source indiscriminately.

Engineer’s takeaway: identity completeness is the product of ADOM-scoped source selection and precedence, not merely successful log ingestion.
lessons.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: per-ADOM Asset Identity Center source selection combines identity clues from FortiGate, FortiClient, FortiMail, FortiWeb, FortiNAC logs and EMS connectors; device-specific source rules override all-device rules; subnet/domain/connector inclusion and exclusion filters
lessons.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Fabric ADOM receives supported telemetry -> data-source rules decide which device/subnet/domain/EMS connector may contribute -> identity and endpoint records are normalized into Asset Identity List -> AD enrichment can add directory context -> dashboards and queries consume the resulting identity view
lessons.evidence_pattern: Asset Identity List source details; per-ADOM Data Sources dialog; source status and device/subnet/domain filters; EMS connector authorization and playbook run; compare source log records to resulting asset/identity rows
lessons.remediation_path: validate Fabric ADOM scope; inspect source enablement and device-specific precedence; add EMS connector as authorized device and enable the sequence playbook when vulnerability data is required; exclude only the noisy device/subnet; verify identity rows after source ingestion
lessons.question_fingerprint: trace an endpoint missing from Asset Identity Center to the per-ADOM source-selection and device-rule precedence rather than log storage
lessons.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: five telemetry source lanes converging through per-ADOM source filters into endpoint and identity normalization, then asset list and dashboard

lessons.title: FortiSwitch flow export: sampling, flow keys, templates, and collector delivery
lessons.summary: FortiSwitch flow export turns sampled packets into NetFlow or IPFIX records. The exporter, template cadence, flow-key level, transport, and model flow limit all affect what the collector can decode.
lessons.body:
Purpose. FortiSwitch flow export provides traffic visibility without sending every packet to a central analyzer. The switch samples packets on ports or trunks, builds flow records from the observed tuples, and exports those records in NetFlow or IPFIX format. It is telemetry, not packet mirroring: a flow record summarizes a conversation and cannot replace a packet capture when payload or exact packet order is required.

Sampling and scope. On a standalone switch, packet sampling is enabled on the selected switch interface. In a FortiLink-managed deployment, the controller can configure sampling on a specific port, all data-receiving perimeter ports, or all ingress ports for hop-by-hop tracking. For perimeter/device-ingress mode, the documented default is one sampled packet out of 512. Local port sampling is different: packet-sample-rate is expressed as packets per second, with a documented default of 512 pps. Keep those two controls distinct when comparing counters or building a sample configuration. ISL/ICL ports are treated specially in perimeter mode.

Flow keys and exported fields. The tracking level determines the information available to the collector. IP level records source/destination IP addresses. Port level adds source/destination ports and protocol. VLAN level includes the IP addresses, ports, protocol, and VLAN. MAC level is available in the FortiSwitchOS flow-export guide for Layer-2 identity. Choose the level that answers the operational question; a lower-detail level cannot be expanded later by the collector. The model defines the maximum number of concurrent flows. When the limit is exceeded, the oldest flow expires and is exported.

Format, templates, and transport. The documented formats include NetFlow v1, v5, v9, and IPFIX. Multiple collectors can be configured with their own IP address, port, and UDP/TCP/SCTP transport. NetFlow commonly uses UDP/2055 and IPFIX UDP/4739, but the actual collector settings must match on both ends. Template packets describe the record fields; the default template export interval is five minutes and can be changed from one to sixty minutes. NetFlow v5 derives its sampling rate from the lowest port number with sampling enabled, so Fortinet recommends consistent sample rates across ports when using v5. Layer-2 flows are not supported for NetFlow v1 or v5.

Example configuration. For a FortiLink-managed switch, enable sampling on a selected port, then configure flow tracking and a collector:

config switch-controller managed-switch
    edit "S524DF4K15000024"
        config ports
            edit "port1"
                set packet-sampler enabled
                set packet-sample-rate 512
                set sample-direction both
            next
        end
    next
end
config switch-controller flow-tracking
    set sample-mode device-ingress
    set sample-rate 512
    set format ipfix
    set level vlan
    set template-export-period 5
    config collectors
        edit "ipfix-collector"
            set ip 192.0.2.50
            set port 4739
            set transport sctp
        next
    end
end

Verification. On managed switches, use diagnose switch-controller flow-collector status and the switch flow-tracking statistics/raw-flow commands. The status output includes exported packet counts, unknown packets, flows, filtered flows, and skipped flowsets. On standalone FortiSwitch, use the get system flow-export-data family and the Flow Export Monitor. On the collector, verify that templates arrive and that records decode with the expected field set.

Troubleshooting example. A collector receives datagrams but displays no usable conversations. Confirm the format and template cadence before increasing the sampling rate. Check whether the selected flow level matches the collector's expected template, whether the transport/port is correct, and whether the switch model supports the feature. A high incompatible-type count can indicate records that the selected NetFlow version cannot export, such as unsupported Layer-2 flows in v1/v5.

Engineer’s takeaway: flow export quality is determined at the switch by sampling, flow-key level, template, timeout, and model capacity—not by the collector alone.
lessons.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: port/trunk packet sampler feeds switch flow cache; configurable sample mode/rate, flow level, NetFlow v1/v5/v9 or IPFIX format, active/inactive protocol timers, templates and one or more collectors using UDP/TCP/SCTP
lessons.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: enable packet sampling on selected ports -> switch aggregates sampled packet tuples into concurrent flow records -> timeout/FIN/RST or table pressure expires records -> exporter emits template plus flowsets to configured collector -> collector decodes fields according to template
lessons.evidence_pattern: diagnose switch-controller flow-collector status; switch flow-tracking statistics and raw records; collector packet capture; template-export-period; Incompatible Type counter
lessons.remediation_path: confirm model support and sampling on ingress/egress ports; choose a supported NetFlow/IPFIX format and flow level; match collector IP/port/transport; ensure templates refresh; account for model flow limits and unsupported L2 records in NetFlow v1/v5
lessons.question_fingerprint: diagnose a collector that receives export packets but cannot decode records by separating template/format mismatch from sampler and transport faults
lessons.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: managed FortiSwitch ports feeding sampler and flow cache, template/flowset exporter, two collectors, separate control path for template refresh

lessons.title: Dynamic VLAN assignment with RADIUS precedence and FortiAP-group pool fallback
lessons.summary: FortiOS 8.0 allows RADIUS dynamic VLAN assignment and VLAN pooling to coexist. The RADIUS VLAN wins when present; the local pool is a deliberate fallback, not a competing assignment method.
lessons.body:
Purpose. Dynamic VLAN assignment places authenticated wireless users into different Layer-2 segments without creating a separate SSID for every user group. FortiAP/FortiWiFi 8.0 supports four assignment methods: RADIUS attributes, Name Tag, FortiAP group, and VLAN pool. The important 8.0 behavior is that Dynamic VLAN and VLAN pooling can be enabled together. Older configuration guidance that says the two methods cannot coexist describes earlier behavior and should not be copied into an 8.0 design without checking the release-specific guide.

Decision order. A client associates to an enterprise SSID and completes RADIUS authentication. If the RADIUS server returns a VLAN in the Tunnel-Private-Group-ID attribute, the wireless controller assigns that VLAN. The standard RADIUS tunnel attributes are Tunnel-Type=VLAN (IETF 64 value 13), Tunnel-Medium-Type=IEEE-802 (IETF 65 value 6), and Tunnel-Private-Group-ID (IETF 81, a VLAN ID from 1–4094). The RADIUS-derived VLAN takes precedence over the local VLAN pool. If the attribute is absent, the controller falls back to the VLAN pool associated with the FortiAP group to which the AP belongs.

Why the fallback is useful. A user-specific RADIUS VLAN is ideal when the identity store knows the user's role. The FortiAP-group pool provides a site/AP-based fallback for authenticated users whose RADIUS record does not include a VLAN. For example, a branch AP group can map such clients to VLAN 10 while a user returned with Tunnel-Private-Group-ID 100 lands in VLAN 100. This avoids treating an absent RADIUS attribute as an authentication failure while preserving explicit user-based placement when the attribute is supplied.

Configuration workflow. Create the RADIUS server and enterprise SSID, enable authentication against that server, then enable Dynamic VLAN. Configure VLAN pooling as wtp-group and map VLAN IDs to FortiAP groups. The Fortinet 8.0 example shows the SSID using WPA2 Enterprise, set dynamic-vlan enable, and set vlan-pooling wtp-group. Create the corresponding VLAN interfaces, addressing/DHCP scopes, and firewall policies on the network path that carries the assigned VLAN. Confirm whether the SSID uses tunnel or local-bridge forwarding; local bridging requires the AP uplink and adjacent switch path to carry the assigned VLAN.

config wireless-controller vap
    edit "corp-enterprise"
        set auth radius
        set radius-server "corp-radius"
        set dynamic-vlan enable
        set vlan-pooling wtp-group
        config vlan-pool
            edit 10
                set wtp-group "branch-east" "branch-west"
            next
            edit 20
                set wtp-group "branch-north"
            next
        end
    next
end

Verification. Inspect the RADIUS Access-Accept for the tunnel attributes. Then use diagnose wireless-controller wlac -d sta online to inspect the station's vlan_id, user, group, AP, and SSID. The Fortinet example shows vlan_id=100(dynamic) when the RADIUS attribute is present and vlan_id=10 when the client receives no Tunnel-Private-Group-ID and falls back to the AP-group pool. Confirm the client also obtains the expected DHCP lease and reaches only the networks allowed by the VLAN's firewall policy.

Troubleshooting example. The user authenticates but lands in the branch default VLAN. Compare the Access-Accept with the station output. If Tunnel-Private-Group-ID is absent, the pool behavior is expected; fix the user/group RADIUS attributes if that user needs a dedicated VLAN. If the station shows the correct VLAN but has no address, investigate VLAN transport, interface tagging, DHCP, and policy rather than changing RADIUS.

Engineer’s takeaway: RADIUS supplies the preferred per-user VLAN; FortiAP-group pooling supplies the documented fallback when that attribute is not returned.
lessons.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiOS 8.0 permits simultaneous Dynamic VLAN and VLAN pooling; RADIUS Access-Accept Tunnel-Private-Group-ID wins; if absent, local pool chooses VLAN by FortiAP group; VLAN interface, DHCP, and policy must exist for each assigned VLAN
lessons.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: client associates to enterprise SSID -> RADIUS authenticates -> Access-Accept returns optional Tunnel-Type/Tunnel-Medium-Type/Tunnel-Private-Group-ID -> controller selects RADIUS VLAN or FortiAP-group pool fallback -> client receives VLAN and DHCP/policy path
lessons.evidence_pattern: RADIUS Access-Accept attributes; diagnose wireless-controller wlac -d sta online vlan_id and group; VLAN interface/DHCP lease; SSID dynamic-vlan and vlan-pooling configuration
lessons.remediation_path: validate the three standard RADIUS tunnel attributes and VLAN ID; create VLAN interfaces, DHCP scopes and firewall policies; verify AP group membership and pool mapping; test one user with and without Tunnel-Private-Group-ID
lessons.question_fingerprint: determine precedence when a user receives a RADIUS VLAN while the AP belongs to a configured VLAN pool
lessons.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: wireless client to AP/controller to RADIUS branch, explicit RADIUS VLAN path above FortiAP-group pool fallback, then VLAN interface/DHCP/policy

lessons.title: FortiNAC agent server discovery: DNS records, certificate identity, and agent-specific connection paths
lessons.summary: FortiNAC agents do not all discover their Application Server in the same way. DNS SRV/TXT records, local configuration, last-connected-server state, ports, and certificate target names must agree.
lessons.body:
Purpose. Endpoint compliance depends on the agent reaching the correct FortiNAC Application Server after it is downloaded or launched. Agent server discovery is the mechanism that tells each agent which server to contact. It is separate from captive-portal reachability: a host can download an agent successfully and still fail its subsequent TLS connection because discovery returned the wrong server name or the certificate does not match the name the agent is using.

Persistent Agent discovery. Persistent Agent 3.x and later can use DNS SRV records plus local registry/preferences/configuration files. It checks the lastConnectedServer value first; a server that has worked before is moved to the top of the candidate list. HomeServer and AllowedServers can also contribute preferred/allowed targets. If restrictRoaming is enabled, the last-connected server remains preferred until it is unreachable. This improves stability for managed endpoints, but it can preserve a stale server choice after a migration unless DNS and the agent's configuration are updated. Persistent Agent 5.3 and later can have SRV lookup disabled, so confirm the agent version and its discovery settings before expecting DNS records to be consulted.

Persistent Agent uses the _bradfordagent._udp and _bradfordagent._tcp SRV records in its discovery process. The Passive Agent follows a different path: a user logon triggers a script served by a corporate server, and the script reads the ServerURL registry entry and tries the listed servers in order. Dissolvable and Mobile Agents use their own AgentConfig discovery path; do not publish one generic record and assume every agent type consumes it.

Certificate identity is part of discovery. Fortinet documents that the Application Server name used by an agent must match the name in the certificate protecting the relevant certificate target. The target depends on the agent type. DNS can resolve correctly and TCP can connect while TLS still fails because the discovered FQDN does not match the certificate SAN/CN or the certificate target expected by the agent. That is why “ping works” is not a sufficient discovery test.

Ports and deployment. Persistent Agent 5.x and later communicates with FortiNAC on TCP 4568; TCP 80 is required for upgrades. Agents distributed through the captive portal are configured automatically to communicate with the server. Agents distributed externally—such as by GPO, software deployment, or a corporate web page—need the correct server settings and DNS records. The Implementation Guide recommends choosing the agent type based on user population: Persistent Agent for daily managed users, Dissolvable Agent for guest workflows, Passive Agent for a managed Windows logon scan, and Mobile Agent for supported mobile registration/inventory functions.

Verification sequence. From an affected endpoint, inspect the relevant registry/preferences/configuration and resolve the expected SRV records. Use nslookup or dig for the documented service names and confirm the returned hostnames also resolve. Verify that the resolved name matches the certificate target and that the required TCP ports are reachable. On the FortiNAC side, compare the agent's configured server and lastConnectedServer with the intended Application Server. Do not diagnose a scan policy until the agent has established its server connection.

Troubleshooting example. A Persistent Agent is installed but never reports a scan. The portal download succeeds, while the agent repeatedly contacts an old server. Inspect lastConnectedServer, restrictRoaming, and whether SRV lookup is disabled, then compare the _bradfordagent SRV answers and certificate name. Correct the authoritative DNS/configuration source, ensure TCP 4568 is reachable, and confirm the agent updates its lastConnectedServer after a successful connection. If upgrades fail while scans work, separately test TCP 80.

Engineer’s takeaway: identify the agent type and version first; its discovery inputs, ports, and certificate target determine the correct troubleshooting path.
lessons.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: agent-type-specific discovery of FortiNAC Application Server using DNS SRV/TXT records, registry/preferences/config files, lastConnectedServer and HomeServer; certificate target name must match discovered server identity; Persistent Agent uses TCP/4568 and TCP/80 for upgrades
lessons.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: agent starts -> reads configured registry/preferences or DNS service records -> builds ordered server candidate list -> resolves host and validates TLS certificate target -> connects to Application Server -> persists lastConnectedServer and optionally restricts roaming
lessons.evidence_pattern: nslookup/dig SRV and TXT records; agent configuration/lastConnectedServer; DNS answer and certificate SAN/CN; TCP 4568/80 reachability; agent/server logs
lessons.remediation_path: verify agent-specific discovery path; publish correct SRV/TXT records in production DNS; ensure DNS alias matches certificate target; confirm TCP 4568 and upgrade TCP 80; clear stale lastConnectedServer or roaming pin only after correcting DNS
lessons.question_fingerprint: separate successful captive-portal download from failed post-download agent-to-Application-Server discovery and certificate validation
lessons.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: four agent types with separate discovery inputs converging on DNS resolution and certificate validation before Application Server connection

lessons.title: SNMPv3 Engine ID caching: why device replacement at the same IP can break polling
lessons.summary: FortiNAC-F caches the SNMPv3 engine ID associated with a network device. Reusing an IP address for replacement hardware can leave a stale engine identity even when the SNMP username and passwords are correct.
lessons.body:
Purpose. FortiNAC-F uses SNMP and CLI credentials to discover, poll, and manage network devices. SNMPv3 User-based Security Model (USM) uses an authoritative engine identity as part of its security processing. FortiNAC caches the engine ID it learned for a device. That cache is normally helpful because the server can continue addressing the same device without rediscovering its identity on every poll. It becomes a problem when the hardware behind an IP address changes.

Failure mechanism. Consider a switch replacement in which the old switch is removed, the replacement receives the same management IP, and the administrator reuses the same SNMPv3 username and authentication/privacy credentials. The replacement switch has a different SNMP engine ID. FortiNAC may still have the old engine ID cached for that IP/device record. The request can therefore fail at the SNMPv3 security layer even though ICMP reachability is good and the credentials appear correct. Repeatedly resetting the SNMP password does not repair a stale engine identity.

Where to inspect it. In Network > Inventory, expand the container, right-click the device, and open Properties. The Credentials tab contains SNMP settings. Select SNMPv3 and verify the username, authentication protocol/password, privacy protocol, and privacy password against the device. FortiNAC-F documents DES and AES-128 as privacy protocol choices for the referenced interface. The Validate Credentials button tests the entered CLI and SNMP credentials. The same Properties view also exposes Clear Cached Engine ID, which clears the stored engine ID and forces a new discovery.

When the device cannot be added. The GUI button is not available if the device has not been successfully added, so Fortinet documents a server-side CLI tool. Log in to the FortiNAC-F server CLI, enter the shell, navigate to /bin, and run:

ClearEngineID -ip 192.0.2.25

Use the actual replacement device's management IP. This is a targeted cache operation; it is not a command to reset the device's SNMP user or change the SNMP engine ID on the switch. After clearing the cache, rediscover the device and validate the credentials again.

Evidence and interpretation. A failed Validate Credentials result is evidence that the management exchange failed; it does not by itself distinguish wrong credentials from stale engine ID, reachability, ACL, or protocol mismatch. Check the device replacement history and whether the IP was reused. Verify the SNMPv3 user and auth/priv settings on the new switch. After the cache clear, a successful validation and a new Last Successful Poll indicate that FortiNAC can communicate with the device again. The System tab's sysName/sysContact/sysLocation fields are obtained from the SNMP System MIB; they can help confirm that the responding device is the intended replacement.

Do not confuse SNMP and CLI credentials. FortiNAC stores SNMP credentials for polling and separate CLI credentials for configuration access. A successful SSH/CLI login does not prove SNMPv3 works, and a successful SNMP poll does not prove the CLI account has write privileges. Test the path that is failing.

Operational example. A switch is replaced during a maintenance window. FortiNAC still shows the device at the old IP but L2/L3 polling stops. Before changing the SNMPv3 user, confirm the replacement and IP reuse, clear the cached engine ID, rediscover, and run Validate Credentials. If polling remains down, then inspect ACLs, SNMP version, authentication/privacy protocol compatibility, and device-side SNMP logs.

Engineer’s takeaway: after same-IP hardware replacement, treat SNMPv3 engine identity as state that may need invalidation—not as another password field.
lessons.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiNAC-F stores SNMPv3 authoritative engine ID discovered for a network device; USM authentication/privacy parameters are evaluated against the engine ID; Clear Cached Engine ID forces discovery of the replacement device's engine ID
lessons.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: device discovery/poll stores engine ID for management IP -> SNMPv3 requests use cached engine identity and configured user/auth/privacy credentials -> replacement at same IP presents a different engine ID -> request fails until cache is cleared and engine discovery is repeated
lessons.evidence_pattern: Network Inventory > device Properties > Credentials; Validate Credentials result; SNMPv3 auth/privacy settings; engine ID cache clear action; ClearEngineID -ip <device IP address>; poll success timestamp
lessons.remediation_path: confirm the device was replaced or IP reused; validate SNMPv3 username/auth/privacy credentials; clear cached engine ID in device properties or run ClearEngineID from the FortiNAC-F server CLI; rediscover and poll before changing credentials
lessons.question_fingerprint: recognize stale SNMPv3 engine ID after same-IP hardware replacement instead of resetting auth/priv passwords
lessons.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiNAC-F credential store with cached engine ID pointing to old switch, IP reused by replacement switch with new engine ID, cache-clear/re-discovery loop

lessons.title: SmartConnect EAP-TLS endpoint binding: using certificate CN to verify the registered MAC device
lessons.summary: FortiAuthenticator 8.0 adds a way to bind a SmartConnect EAP-TLS client certificate to a registered endpoint MAC address. RADIUS can reject a valid certificate when the connecting device does not match the certificate's CN.
lessons.body:
Purpose. EAP-TLS proves possession of a client private key and validates a certificate chain, but certificate trust alone does not necessarily prove that the endpoint presenting the certificate is the device that was registered to the user. FortiAuthenticator 8.0 adds a SmartConnect option that can place a registered MAC Device value in the client certificate's subject CN, plus a RADIUS policy control that compares the MAC address received from the RADIUS client with that CN.

Enrollment and authentication flow. In Authentication > Portals > Smart Connect Profiles, create a profile for WPA2 Enterprise/EAP-TLS. The new Client certificate CN dropdown lets the administrator select the user account attribute used as the certificate CN; the new MAC Device choice binds the CN to a registered MAC device rather than always using the username. The user must have a MAC device registered through the portal/device-management workflow. When device management is enabled and the user reaches the allowed device limit, the portal can ask the user to replace an existing device. When device management is disabled, a new unregistered MAC can be denied instead of silently replacing an old registration.

The endpoint then presents the provisioned certificate during EAP-TLS. The RADIUS client sends the endpoint MAC in the Access-Request (commonly as Calling-Station-Id, depending on the NAS). In Authentication > RADIUS Service > Policies, the EAP-TLS policy exposes Verify MAC address in CN of client certificate, disabled by default. When enabled, FortiAuthenticator compares the MAC sent by the RADIUS client with the CN in the certificate subject. A trusted certificate can therefore be rejected if the endpoint identity does not match the registered device.

Configuration dependencies. First enable the portal's device tracking/management behavior appropriate to the user experience. Then create the SmartConnect profile and select MAC Device for the certificate CN. Finally, enable MAC-to-CN verification in the relevant EAP-TLS RADIUS policy. Confirm that the RADIUS client actually sends the endpoint MAC and that the certificate is issued with the expected normalized value. If the portal is configured for tracking-only, management-only, or both, understand what each mode permits: tracking records the device; management controls replacement/selection behavior. The post-login Devices menu appears only when device management is enabled.

Verification. Inspect the SmartConnect profile and the issued certificate subject. Capture or inspect the RADIUS Access-Request to identify the exact MAC attribute and formatting. Check the RADIUS policy's verification toggle and the authentication log. A certificate-chain success proves that the issuer and validity checks passed; it does not prove the MAC-to-CN comparison passed. Conversely, a MAC/CN mismatch is not repaired by reissuing the same certificate with the same CN.

Troubleshooting example. A user authenticates successfully on a previously enrolled laptop but receives an EAP-TLS rejection on a replacement laptop. The new laptop presents a valid certificate copied from the old device, while the RADIUS client reports a different MAC. With verification enabled, that mismatch is the intended security boundary. Register the replacement device, issue/select a certificate whose CN represents the new MAC, and retest. If the certificate is correct but authentication still fails, compare the RADIUS client's MAC formatting and confirm that the policy being matched is the one with the verification option.

Security and operational caveats. MAC addresses are identifiers, not cryptographic secrets. The control binds a certificate to the MAC value reported by the network access device; it does not make MAC spoofing impossible. It is strongest when combined with trusted EAP-TLS certificate issuance, controlled portal enrollment, and network-device integrity. Maintain a clear replacement process so legitimate hardware swaps do not become an uncontrolled exception path.

Engineer’s takeaway: certificate validation and endpoint binding are separate checks; verify both the certificate CN and the MAC attribute received by RADIUS.
lessons.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Smart Connect profile chooses client-certificate subject CN from user account attribute or registered MAC Device; EAP-TLS RADIUS policy can require endpoint MAC from RADIUS client to equal certificate subject CN; portal device tracking/management controls enrollment and replacement
lessons.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: user registers/selects a MAC device in portal -> SmartConnect provisions EAP-TLS client certificate with CN bound to selected MAC -> supplicant presents certificate in EAP-TLS -> RADIUS policy validates certificate and compares request MAC to CN -> access accepted only when identity binding matches
lessons.evidence_pattern: Smart Connect profile Client certificate CN setting; certificate subject CN; RADIUS Access-Request Calling-Station-Id; EAP-TLS policy Verify MAC address in CN; RADIUS accept/reject logs
lessons.remediation_path: enable device tracking/management as intended; choose MAC Device CN; ensure portal user has registered MAC; enable RADIUS MAC-to-CN verification; normalize MAC formatting and confirm the RADIUS client sends the correct endpoint MAC
lessons.question_fingerprint: distinguish certificate-chain validity from endpoint identity binding when EAP-TLS certificate is trusted but MAC/CN comparison fails
lessons.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: portal device registration feeding certificate enrollment, EAP-TLS supplicant to RADIUS policy, certificate CN and Calling-Station-Id comparison gate

lessons.title: Access Authentication: step-up authentication and time-bounded authorization for a secret
lessons.summary: Access Authentication adds a reauthentication gate before a user can access a secret. It is distinct from approval-to-launch and checkout: it establishes a time-limited authentication window.
lessons.body:
Purpose. A user may have permission to see a secret in FortiPAM but still be required to authenticate again before using it. The secret's Access Authentication setting adds that step-up gate. It is useful when a privileged credential is visible to an operator for routine workflow but access should require a fresh authentication event close to the time of use.

Where it lives. Open Secrets > Secrets, select the secret, and use its Settings tab. Under Session Security, enable Access Authentication. The secret can be associated with a remote authentication server and a validity duration. The documented default duration is 60 minutes; the allowed range is 0–180 minutes. A duration of 0 means a short-lived authorization for immediate use, effectively limited to one secret. FortiPAM displays Access Authentication Status and the remaining time for which the user has access.

Transaction flow. The user opens a secret. FortiPAM evaluates the effective policy and determines whether access authentication is required. If so, the user completes the configured authentication before the secret's protected operations are enabled. The resulting authorization is time-bounded. When the window expires, the user must authenticate again. This gate is not the same as an approval profile: approval asks an approver to authorize a launch or job; Access Authentication asks the user to prove identity again. It is also not checkout, which grants one user exclusive use of a secret for a limited period.

Policy inheritance and bypass. A folder policy can set Access Authentication to Enable, Disable, or Not Set. When the policy forces Enable or Disable, the secret cannot override that setting; Not Set allows the secret-level value to control the behavior. Inspect the parent folder policy before assuming the secret's toggle is authoritative. The Bypass For Owners option is disabled by default. Enabling it creates a privileged exception for the owner, so document the reason and test it explicitly. Do not confuse ownership with successful step-up authentication; an owner bypass is a policy exception, not an authentication result.

Configuration example. For a sensitive network-device secret, enable Access Authentication, select the appropriate remote server, and set a duration that matches the risk and operational task. A 15-minute window may suit a short maintenance action; a longer window may be justified for a controlled troubleshooting session. Use 0 only when the intended behavior is immediate, one-secret use. Keep owner bypass disabled unless the control owner has approved that exception.

Verification. Open the secret as a user who has permission but has not recently authenticated. Confirm that FortiPAM requires authentication and that protected editing/launch behavior is unavailable until authentication succeeds. After success, inspect Access Authentication Status and the remaining duration. Wait for expiry or use a test account to verify that the gate returns. Check audit records to correlate the user, secret, authentication event, and subsequent access.

Troubleshooting example. An operator can browse a secret but cannot edit its settings or launch it. Do not immediately change the user's role. First check whether Access Authentication is enabled, whether the authentication server is reachable, whether the user's authentication window has expired, and whether the folder policy forces the setting. If the user was approved to launch the secret but still sees an authentication prompt, that can be correct: approval and step-up authentication are independent controls.

Security considerations. The duration trades friction against exposure. Longer windows reduce repeated prompts but increase the time a stolen authenticated session may retain access. Zero-minute mode is intentionally restrictive. Owner bypass should be treated as a documented exception, not a convenience default. Session recording, proxy mode, clipboard controls, approval, checkout, and ZTNA control are separate settings; Access Authentication does not replace them.

Engineer’s takeaway: use Access Authentication for fresh identity proof, approval for delegated authorization, and checkout for exclusive secret use.
lessons.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: secret-level Access Authentication requires user authentication before secret access; remote authentication server selection; configurable validity duration 0-180 minutes with default 60; duration 0 gives immediate-use short-lived authorization; owner bypass is separately controlled
lessons.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: user opens secret -> FortiPAM evaluates inherited folder/secret settings -> if Access Authentication required, user completes configured authentication -> FortiPAM grants time-bounded access window -> secret operations are enabled only while authorization is valid
lessons.evidence_pattern: secret Settings > Access Authentication; selected remote server; duration and bypass fields; Access Authentication Status remaining time; user/session audit logs
lessons.remediation_path: confirm folder inheritance and secret override; validate remote authentication server; choose a duration matching risk; keep owner bypass disabled unless explicitly approved; test expiration and 0-minute single-use behavior
lessons.question_fingerprint: distinguish approval-to-launch from step-up Access Authentication and select the correct control for expiring authorization
lessons.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: user request enters folder policy inheritance then secret-level step-up authentication, timed authorization gate, secret launch and expiry loop

lessons.title: FortiSIEM Manager: multi-instance incident control, telemetry cadence, and on-demand raw-event retrieval
lessons.summary: FortiSIEM Manager is a separately licensed central management plane for multiple FortiSIEM instances. It stores incident and health metadata, but retrieves raw triggering events from the source instance when an analyst opens them.
lessons.body:
Purpose and architecture. FortiSIEM Manager lets an organization monitor and manage multiple FortiSIEM instances from a separate virtual machine. It requires its own license. The User Guide documents support for FortiSIEM Manager and Supervisor instances at version 6.5.0 or later. Each FortiSIEM instance must register with the Manager; successful registration establishes a bidirectional HTTP(S) communication channel using REST APIs. This is a control/management plane, not a central raw-event lake.

What is forwarded and when. Incidents are forwarded in near-real time. Health information is forwarded once per minute, and license information once per hour. The Manager retains the last one day of health information and stores incidents plus the latest license information in its local PostgreSQL database. The number of incidents it can retain depends on the size of that database. Raw events are not stored in the Manager. When an analyst opens the Triggering Event tab for an incident, the Manager fetches the raw events on demand from the FortiSIEM instance where the incident occurred.

Control actions and context. Incident status changes in each instance are forwarded to the Manager. New or modified rules are also forwarded. From the Manager, an operator can clear, resolve, or comment on incidents; disable rules or change their severity; change incident severity; and run FortiSOAR playbooks/connectors. The Manager propagates the operation to the correct instance with the logged-in Manager user's context. That means the central interface does not erase the source instance's authorization model. An operator should still verify that the intended instance and permissions are correct.

Registration and upgrade sequence. Install the Manager on a separate supported VM, apply its separate license, and register each target instance. Confirm that the bidirectional HTTP(S) channel is established. Fortinet explicitly requires upgrading the Manager before upgrading the FortiSIEM instances, for both content updates and software image updates. Reversing that order can leave the management plane behind the instances it is expected to control.

Verification. Check that each instance is registered and that its health timestamp advances at the expected one-minute cadence. License information updates hourly, so a few minutes of delay is not evidence of a failed channel. Confirm that an incident appears centrally and that status changes propagate back to the source. When an analyst opens Triggering Event, the Manager must reach the source instance to retrieve raw events; inspect that instance's availability and the REST/HTTP(S) path if the event detail is unavailable.

Operational example. A SOC analyst sees an incident in the Manager but the Triggering Event tab is empty. The wrong assumption is that the Manager's PostgreSQL database is corrupt or has lost raw logs. The documented design is that raw events are fetched from the source instance on demand. Verify the incident's origin instance, its registration/channel health, and its event retention/query availability. The Manager can still display the incident metadata even when the source instance cannot answer the raw-event request.

Capacity and retention implications. Do not size the Manager as if it were a second full SIEM event store. Its health retention is one day, and incident retention is constrained by local PostgreSQL capacity. Raw-event retention, event database sizing, and search performance remain responsibilities of the source FortiSIEM deployment. Central visibility does not eliminate per-instance lifecycle planning.

Engineer’s takeaway: use the Manager for cross-instance incident operations and health/license oversight; use the originating instance for raw event evidence.
lessons.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: separate licensed Manager VM registers FortiSIEM 6.5+ instances; registration creates bidirectional HTTP(S) REST channel; incidents near-real-time, health every minute, license hourly; Manager stores incidents/license/one day health in local PostgreSQL but not raw events
lessons.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: instance registers to Manager -> secure two-way REST channel forwards incident/status/rule changes and periodic health/license -> central operator changes incident or rule state -> Manager propagates action with logged-in user context -> raw triggering events are fetched on demand from originating instance
lessons.evidence_pattern: Manager instance registration status; REST/HTTP(S) connectivity; health timestamp cadence; PostgreSQL incident/license records; triggering-event request to originating instance; upgrade sequencing
lessons.remediation_path: install separately licensed Manager VM; register supported 6.5+ instances; validate bidirectional HTTP(S) and REST access; upgrade Manager before instances; troubleshoot raw-event retrieval at source instance rather than expecting Manager to store raw events
lessons.question_fingerprint: identify why an incident appears centrally while raw triggering events are unavailable: Manager stores incident metadata but fetches raw events from the source instance on demand
lessons.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: three FortiSIEM instances sending incident/health/license lanes to separate Manager PostgreSQL store, with on-demand raw-event pullback to selected source

lessons.title: Agent-based Entra ID SAML SSO: claims, certificates, group limits, and stable egress identity
lessons.summary: FortiSASE acts as the SAML service provider for FortiClient agent-based tunnel login. The SAML redirect, claim mapping, certificate lifecycle, group assertion limit, and client public IP stability all affect whether the tunnel can authenticate.
lessons.body:
Purpose. FortiSASE can use Microsoft Entra ID as a SAML identity provider for FortiClient agent-based tunnel authentication. The user signs in with Entra ID credentials and, if configured, Entra MFA. FortiSASE is the service provider (SP). The feature is more than a certificate upload: the SP/IdP identifiers, assertion consumer endpoint, claims, group mapping, and client network path must all agree.

Control-plane transaction. In FortiSASE, go to Configuration > VPN User SSO and start the SSO wizard. Copy the FortiSASE entity ID, SSO URL, and single-logout values. In Entra ID, create the FortiSASE enterprise application, choose SAML, enter the SP values in Identifier/Entity ID, Reply URL/ACS, Sign-on URL, and Logout URL, and assign the intended users and groups. Download the Entra ID SAML signing certificate and copy the IdP entity ID, login URL, and logout URL back into FortiSASE.

Claims and certificates. Map the username and group claim names to the claim names configured in Entra ID. Import the IdP signing certificate into FortiSASE. Select the SP certificate and digest method; when Entra ID verifies the SP signature, the digest method must match on both sides. FortiSASE's built-in default certificate is shared across its points of presence and renews periodically. If the IdP pins the SP certificate, administrators may need to update the IdP configuration when the default certificate renews. Fortinet recommends using a custom SP certificate when avoiding periodic IdP certificate updates is important.

Group and path constraints. FortiSASE cannot retrieve a user's Entra ID group membership if the user belongs to more than 150 groups. Filter the Entra ID group claim to send only relevant groups. There is also a network-path constraint: SAML authentication can fail if traffic between the agent and the IdP is load-balanced across changing public source IP addresses. All traffic from the agent to the SAML IdP must use one unique public IP that does not change during the SAML transaction. A client-side SD-WAN or internet load balancer can break the redirect even when the IdP is healthy.

Authentication precedence. The current guide notes that enabling SSO authentication takes priority over existing LDAP and RADIUS authentication methods. Plan the transition before enabling it for production users. Configure Entra MFA in Entra ID for the intended users; FortiSASE supports the Entra MFA prompt during FortiClient login. Do not assume that an LDAP fallback will be used after SAML is enabled.

Verification. On the endpoint, FortiClient's Remote Access view should display the SAML Login action. Test with a controlled user and observe the redirect to Entra ID, MFA if required, and return assertion to FortiSASE. Confirm that the username and group claims map to the intended user/group. Compare the IdP and SP certificates and digest method. Record the client's public IP before and during the redirect; it must remain stable. A successful Entra sign-in page proves only that the user authenticated at the IdP, not that FortiSASE accepted the assertion or matched the correct group.

Troubleshooting example. Users complete Entra MFA but FortiClient returns to the login page. Check the ACS/Reply URL and entity ID first, then certificate and digest alignment, claim names, and group count. If only users behind a multi-WAN branch fail, capture the public egress IP across the redirect. Pin the SAML IdP traffic to one stable public IP for the transaction rather than changing group policy to compensate for a broken SAML exchange.

Engineer’s takeaway: troubleshoot SAML as a complete redirect transaction: identifiers, signatures, claims, group size, and stable source IP.
lessons.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Entra ID IdP issues SAML assertion to FortiSASE SP for FortiClient agent-based tunnel; username/group claim mapping, IdP signing cert, SP certificate, digest selection, optional group matching; group membership retrieval limit of 150; IdP transaction requires stable public source IP
lessons.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: FortiClient SAML login -> redirect to Entra ID -> user/MFA authentication -> signed assertion returned to FortiSASE ACS -> certificate/digest and claims validated -> group mapping and VPN authorization -> tunnel established
lessons.evidence_pattern: SAML Entity ID/ACS/SLS values; IdP certificate and digest; username/group claim mapping; group assertion count; FortiClient SAML login trace; client public IP stability across IdP redirect
lessons.remediation_path: copy exact SP entity/ACS/SLS values; map username and group claims; use a stable custom SP certificate where practical; filter Entra group claims to 150 or fewer; ensure all IdP traffic uses one stable public IP during login
lessons.question_fingerprint: diagnose SAML login that authenticates at Entra but fails at FortiSASE because source IP changes during redirect or group claim exceeds 150
lessons.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiClient to Entra IdP redirect and signed assertion return to FortiSASE SP, with certificate/claim/group validation and stable-egress constraint

lessons.title: SD-WAN multicast steering: PIM control traffic, SLA failover, and ADVPN shortcut boundaries
lessons.summary: FortiOS can steer IPv4 and IPv6 multicast traffic through SD-WAN rules. PIM must use the SD-WAN decision, and ADVPN shortcuts must be disabled for the multicast service.
lessons.body:
Purpose. SD-WAN service rules can steer multicast traffic as well as unicast application traffic. This matters for hub-and-spoke designs in which a multicast source or rendezvous point (RP) is reachable through more than one overlay tunnel. When the selected member becomes out of SLA, multicast traffic can fail over to another member and return when the preferred path recovers. This is not achieved by adding a generic “multicast” address object; PIM control traffic must participate in the SD-WAN path decision.

PIM integration. Fortinet documents the pim-use-sdwan option under config router multicast or config router multicast6. It controls whether PIM uses SD-WAN when checking RP neighbors and sending packets. For IPv4, configure it under config router multicast > config pim-sm-global; for IPv6, use config router multicast6 > config pim-sm-global. Enable multicast routing, configure the RP, and enable PIM sparse mode on the relevant source, receiver, and overlay interfaces.

SD-WAN service rule. Add the overlay tunnel interfaces as SD-WAN members and create a Performance SLA health check to a reachable hub/RP target. Create a service rule for PIM protocol 103, use the SLA strategy, reference the health check, and specify the preferred member order. The Fortinet example uses set protocol 103, an SLA rule, and set priority-members to define the path preference. The PIM control packets and the multicast stream must use a coherent path; a health check that monitors only an unrelated internet destination may not represent the RP path.

ADVPN constraint. Fortinet explicitly states that ADVPN is not supported when SD-WAN steers multicast traffic. Disable shortcuts on the multicast service with set shortcut disable and disable shortcut-SLA use for the same rule where required by the release-specific example. This is an architectural boundary: do not combine multicast steering and dynamic ADVPN shortcut formation on the same service and expect the control plane to behave as if it were a normal unicast application.

config router multicast
    set multicast-routing enable
    config pim-sm-global
        set pim-use-sdwan enable
        config rp-address
            edit 1
                set ip-address 172.16.205.1
            next
        end
    end
end
config system sdwan
    config service
        edit 1
            set mode sla
            set protocol 103
            set priority-members 1 2
            set shortcut disable
            set use-shortcut-sla disable
        next
    end
end

Verification. Check PIM sparse-mode neighbors and multicast route/group state, then inspect diagnose sys sdwan health-check for each overlay member. The documentation example shows one tunnel in SLA and another available as the alternate; when the preferred tunnel crosses its loss/latency threshold, multicast traffic moves to the alternate and returns when the first path recovers. Verify both control-plane adjacency and actual receiver traffic. A green unicast ping SLA does not prove that PIM joins, RP reachability, or multicast forwarding are correct.

Troubleshooting example. The receiver stops getting a stream after the preferred overlay fails, although the alternate tunnel is up. Check whether PIM is enabled on the tunnel interfaces, whether the RP is reachable through the selected service, whether pim-use-sdwan is enabled, and whether the rule matches protocol 103. Confirm that shortcut is disabled for the multicast rule. Then inspect the PIM neighbor table and multicast route state before changing the SLA thresholds.

IPv6 and design caveats. Fortinet's 7.6.0 New Features Guide adds IPv6 multicast steering using config router multicast6. The same design discipline applies: define the IPv6 RP, PIM interfaces, IPv6 multicast policy, service rule, and SLA. Keep source, RP, receiver, and return-path design explicit; multicast routing state is not inferred solely from an SD-WAN member being alive.

Engineer’s takeaway: multicast failover requires PIM-to-SD-WAN integration and a protocol-specific service rule; health-check status alone is insufficient evidence.
lessons.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: SD-WAN service rules classify PIM protocol 103 and steer IPv4/IPv6 multicast; pim-use-sdwan makes PIM RP-neighbor checks and control packets use SD-WAN; SLA member failover moves multicast stream; ADVPN shortcuts are unsupported and must be disabled for the multicast service
lessons.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: receiver joins multicast group -> PIM-SM control traffic reaches RP through selected overlay member -> SLA monitors hub/RP path -> failed member removes multicast path and SD-WAN selects alternate member -> stream continues and returns to preferred member after SLA recovery
lessons.evidence_pattern: diagnose sys sdwan health-check; PIM sparse-mode neighbor table; multicast route/group state; service rule protocol 103; pim-use-sdwan; shortcut disable; packet capture on both overlay members
lessons.remediation_path: enable multicast routing and PIM on relevant interfaces; configure RP; enable pim-use-sdwan; add protocol 103 SD-WAN service with SLA and priority members; disable shortcut for that service; verify PIM neighbor and stream failover separately
lessons.question_fingerprint: explain why a healthy unicast SLA does not prove multicast control-plane path selection and identify the required PIM/SD-WAN integration
lessons.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: multicast source and RP behind dual-hub, two overlay members to spoke receiver, PIM control-plane path through SD-WAN selector and SLA failover
